speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Just to recap, Phase Three is not a return to the pre-COVID-19 status quo, but a new normal which will last until such time the rest of the world also has the virus under tight control or when effective treatments or vaccines are widely available.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must prepare ourselves for a Phase Three that could last for a prolonged period – potentially a year or more.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In this context, we need to put in place the measures and equip ourselves with the tools which will enable us to stay safe, as we allow greater flexibility to live, work and even celebrate major life events.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In determining the capacity limits for events in Phase Three, we took into account various factors such as the frequency at which the activity takes place, the potential risk factors inherent to the nature of the event and whether additional safety measures can be effectively put in place to limit or mitigate these risks.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our analysis of how COVID-19 transmission takes place indicates that the probability of transmission tends to be higher in social settings.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In Singapore, we saw large clusters forming due to the SAFRA Jurong dinner and the Mei Hwan Drive condominium family get-together which took place over Chinese New Year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is natural to lower our guard when we are among family and friends.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: When we have meals together, the risk is higher as masks must be removed while eating and drinking.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Many of us go out for meals practically every day and with different groups, the risk is multiplied many times.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Taking banquet tables as an example, many used to seat around 10 people before COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: So, eight persons is about the maximum that these tables can take while allowing some additional distancing compared to the past.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As the World Health Organization puts it, any size of gathering poses a risk of COVID-19 transmission.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: That is why many countries facing a surge in COVID-19 infections have had to impose lockdowns and prohibit social gatherings.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But disallowing social gatherings for prolonged period of time is not tenable nor desirable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: So, while we now allow social gatherings, we should still limit our circle of close contacts to reduce the risk of spread to a large number of people if an infected person happens to be in the group.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, allowing gatherings of up to eight in Phase Three, strikes a careful balance between maintaining safe distancing and allowing large groups to come together.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In settings where safe management measures can be effectively imposed to mitigate risks and where interactions between different groups can be managed, we can allow a higher capacity limit, especially for important events.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Weddings, for example, are key milestones in life, where friends and family come together to celebrate this joyous occasion.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These, however, are high risk settings, as friends and family would naturally have the tendency to want to socialise and mix across groups and often unmasked as we allow food and drinks too.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For such high risk events, we will need to put in place additional measures to ensure that they can be conducted safely.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, guests are already not supposed to mingle beyond their groups of five at their table and they must use SafeEntry and TraceTogether.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This allows more family and friends to participate, while still minimising the total number of interactions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Given the need for a short turnaround time for such testing prior to the events, we are using alternative test kits such as antigen rapid tests which can return fairly accurate results quickly, within half an hour or so.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, they are not as accurate as the Polymerase Chain Reaction or PCR tests which remains the definitive test for the confirmation of COVID-19 cases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As such, while pre-event testing helps to reduce the probability that a COVID-positive case is present at the event, it cannot eliminate it totally, and safe management measures will still have to be observed at the event.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Another key enabler is a enhanced contact tracing capability.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are progressively rolling out TraceTogether-only SafeEntry to ensure that all those who are visiting places where they are likely to be in contact with many others for prolonged periods, or where human traffic is high, have the TraceTogether App or Token.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is to speed up contact tracing efforts should someone you had been in close contact with at the event become a COVID-19 patient, and to allow us to provide you with medical care early if you become infected.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Government will continue to work with businesses and premise owners to ensure that they maintain the appropriate safe management measures, and regularly remind their employees and associates to comply with these measures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our Safe Distancing Ambassadors and Enforcement Officers will be on the ground to advise the public on safe distancing measures and take enforcement actions where necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must set the right spirit across society and make sure all of us remain committed to maintaining the discipline that will keep us safe, even if we progress to Phase Three.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In fact, even more so when we progress to Phase Three.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: If we can put in place more enablers and risk-mitigating measures that allow for further opening and scaling up of activities, we will.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On the other hand, if and where conditions worsen, we will take targeted measures too.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must not let our guard down and become lax in adherence to safe management measures, as so doing could result in a resurgence of COVID-19 cases, putting all our sacrifices thus far to waste.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have set up our defences at our borders, so that even as we welcome business partners and friends from overseas back to Singapore, we will be able to do so safely.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Should there be a spike in cases, we need to respond swiftly and decisively.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We cannot rule out the need to re-impose measures or introduce new measures in order to keep the virus under control.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Together, we will arrive at Phase Three and emerge stronger ultimately.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some do not want to attend the large-scale events, even weddings because of their fear of doing the tests.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Couples have given feedback that some of the elderly and their guests will actually decline the wedding invitations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They are saying it is actually like restaurant dining, but just that there are 10 tables of five each and the rule of no inter-table mingling is allowed as well.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can that be considered as the way for weddings?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is a question that the taskforce has debated to and fro, and we have decided that we need to calibrate our measures very carefully.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We do understand the concerns of guests including the wedding party.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we have to bear in mind that wedding dinners are quite different from a similar dinner at a restaurant.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If you go to a restaurant with, say, 10 tables with five persons each, that would be 50.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is quite different from a wedding dinner reception with 50 people.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Because if you do go to a restaurant with 10 tables of five each, chances are not all of them know each other.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The intermingling between the tables is very minimal.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We do allow families now to go together and book two tables, but we also encourage them to minimise intermingling.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But at a wedding reception, it is quite different.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Even before you go into the wedding dinner, they will be socialising outside the event and in the banquet hall.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Even if you try to enforce, it is very difficult.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: You really do not want to have to stop the wedding, disrupt the wedding and issue them summons, while the wedding is on-going.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is something that we need to calibrate very carefully.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And also bearing in mind that in the wedding environment, we do expect the wedding couple to take pictures with different tables, different groups.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We also try to mitigate the risk exposure, as they do so.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There are some rules  but it is not possible to prohibit photo-taking.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we understand the needs of the wedding couple and we try to accommodate, but the risk factor is quite different from a normal dinner.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: On top of that, all of us who have attended wedding dinners also know that wedding dinners sometimes can stretch to a couple of hours or even longer, whereas a normal dinner tends to be much shorter.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, although they may seem similar, actually the risk factors are quite different.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And this has also been borne out in the wedding celebrations in other countries that we have seen, that have culminated into big clusters.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We do understand that the pre-event testing, antigen rapid tests, can be frightening and scary.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: That is why we are doing pilot testing to make sure that it is reasonably comfortable.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But, of course, there is still some inconvenience that you have to face with.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If you are tested positive, unfortunately, your plan to attend the wedding may be squashed.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, for the couple, we encourage them to go for testing even before the day of the wedding dinner because you do not really want to disrupt the couple themselves if they were already at the dinner.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, be assured that we are looking at this quite thoroughly.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, this is the current rule on weddings.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If we were to do so, we have to seriously consider whether we will require pre-event testing for such gatherings.
